claim: Of SIPs registered in calendar 2023, only 18.2M of 34.8M were still active at 31 Dec 2024 (48% closed within 1-2 years of registration)
value: 48% closed (52% surviving)
unit: % of SIP registrations (count) closed by end of following year; cohort age 12-24 months at measurement
population: All Indian mutual-fund SIP registrations in calendar 2023 (all ticket sizes, mostly monthly SIPs)
source_title: Business Standard: SIP account openings surge, but premature closures also on the rise (Amfi data)
notes: ANALOGUE, not a daily gold save: monthly SIPs of mostly salaried, wealthier investors. Method: 2023 registrations vs AMFI count of SIPs aged 1-2 yrs at 31-Dec-2024 (via search snippet + AngelOne/Magzter reprints; BS page 403). Survival ~52% at ~18 months average age vs our gig base 20% at 12m - mainstream SIPs are 2-3x stickier than our base. BUT registrations are inflated by 'SIP edit' re-registrations (article says so), which overstates closures, so true SIP survival is even higher. Our population is poorer and paid daily; do not read this as support for raising our base, read it as the CEILING.

claim: Of 25.7M SIPs registered in 2022, 42% had closed by end-2023
value: 42% closed (58% surviving)
unit: % of SIP registrations (count) closed within 1-2 years
population: All Indian MF SIP registrations in calendar 2022
source_title: Business Standard: SIP account openings surge, but premature closures also on the rise (Amfi data)
notes: ANALOGUE. Same method as previous row. Closure rate rising year on year (42% -> 48%) as SIPs spread to newer, smaller investors - the direction our segment sits in.

claim: AMFI full-year SIP stoppage ratio: FY25 514.17 lakh SIPs discontinued vs 679.85 lakh new (75.63%); FY26 679.75 lakh discontinued/matured vs 719.22 lakh new, distorted by an AMFI clean-up that removed ~1.43 crore defunct SIP folios
value: 75.63% (FY25); FY26 not clean
unit: discontinued-or-matured SIPs / new SIP registrations, per year (count)
population: All Indian MF SIP accounts
source_title: Business Today (FY25 stoppage 75.63%) and Finnovate blog (FY26 totals) via search summaries
notes: Same AMFI monthly series as NG-036. A BOOK ratio (stops / new starts), not cohort survival: it cannot be turned into month-12 survival without vintage data. Included to stop anyone quoting 'stoppage ratio 75%' as 'SIP survival 25%' - it is not. FY26 figures are search-summary only and include matured SIPs and a one-off folio clean-up.

claim: Chhoti SIPs (Rs 250, first-time investors) monthly closures were 34,000 in April 2025 on a base of 1.97 lakh, and 26,000 in May 2026 on a base of about 3.2 lakh
value: ~17% (Apr-2025) and ~8% (May-2026) of the book closing per month (derived)
unit: closures per month / live Chhoti SIP count (derived)
population: All Chhoti SIPs across AMCs, India
source_title: Business Standard: Chhoti SIPs gain scale but face high exit rush amid West Asia conflict
notes: Same article as NG-033/NG-034; the per-month ratio is my derivation. A BOOK churn of 8%/month on a book that already contains survivors means a fresh cohort churns faster than 8%/month early on. Our gig base implies ~12.5%/month average to month 12 (100->20). Consistent with our base, not with bull. The Morning Context (8 Jul 2026, paywalled) headlined that Chhoti SIP 'doesn't seem to have caught on' - body not readable.

claim: Regular-instalment commitment savings product (weekly fixed deposits to a self-chosen goal, 3-6 months, self-chosen penalty if 2+ deposits behind): 27% of offered households took it up; 55% of those who took it up defaulted on their savings contract
value: 27% take-up; 55% defaulted (45% completed)
unit: % of offered households; % of product clients (count) completing a 3-6 month plan
population: 913 low- and middle-income households, Gingoog City and Camiguin, Philippines, 2011-2013 (RCT)
source_title: IPA: When Commitment Fails - Evidence from an Installment Savings Product in the Philippines (Anett John; published Management Science 2020)
notes: Closest RCT analogue to a scheduled small regular save. 45% kept going to a 3-6 month goal vs our gig base 48% at m3 / 33% at m6. Deposits were MANUAL (client had to show up), our debits are AUTOMATIC, which should help; but our users are paid daily and volatile. People underestimated their self-control problems and chose weak commitments (author). Self-selected: only 27% wanted it.

claim: Free savings accounts offered to unbanked households: over two years only 17% (Uganda), 10% (Malawi) and 3% (Chile) of those offered made five or more deposits
unit: % of treatment individuals (offered, not opened) making 5+ deposits in 2 years
population: Unbanked households offered free basic accounts in Uganda, Malawi and Chile (RCTs)
source_title: Dupas, Karlan, Robinson & Ubfal, 'Banking the Unbanked? Evidence from Three Countries', AEJ: Applied 10(2) 2018 (CGD WP 440 summary)
notes: Denominator is everyone OFFERED, not activated savers, so not directly comparable to our ret_m24 (activated base). The point it makes: a savings product handed to low-income people mostly goes dormant, even when it is free and convenient; sustained use is the exception (3-17%). Those who did use it saved a lot (79th-96th percentile of baseline savings). No auto-debit. Reinforces that 10% of ACTIVATED at 24m is not conservative once you count drop-off before activation.

claim: SEED commitment savings account: 28% of those offered opened one; after twelve months about half of clients had deposited beyond the opening deposit and one third regularly made deposits
value: 28% take-up; ~50% any later deposit; ~33% regular depositors at 12 months
unit: % of offered (take-up); % of SEED account holders (count) at 12 months
population: 1,777 existing clients of Green Bank of Caraga, Butuan City, Philippines, 2003-2004 (RCT)
source_title: J-PAL: Commitment Savings Products in the Philippines (Ashraf, Karlan & Yin, QJE 2006)
notes: 33% 'regularly made deposits' at 12 months among account OPENERS vs our gig base 20% at 12m. But SEED users were existing bank clients (already banked, more stable) and deposits were manual into a locked box; our users are newer to formal finance with volatile daily income. Upper-end analogue: supports our BULL (32%) more than base, and would argue the self-employed base (25%) is not too high.

claim: Free savings accounts for low-income micro-entrepreneurs in Chile: 53% of those offered opened one, 39% made deposits beyond the minimum or later transactions; access to savings cut informal borrowing (family/friends debt index -36%, service-provider debt -24%)
value: 53% opened; 39% active; -36% / -24% borrowing
unit: % of offered (count); % change in debt indices vs control
population: 3,500+ low-income micro-entrepreneurs, clients of Fondo Esperanza microfinance, Chile (RCT, 12 months)
source_title: J-PAL: Savings Accounts to Smooth Consumption for Low-Income Microentrepreneurs in Chile (Kast & Pomeranz)
notes: Retention: 39/53 = 74% of openers used it beyond the minimum (no time profile). For CROSS-SELL this is the important bit: when poor micro-entrepreneurs get a savings buffer they BORROW LESS. That cuts against loan_apply: savers self-insure. Peer-group meetings doubled balances (supports the 'savings buddy' channel); a 5% interest rate had no effect.

claim: No published statistic found on recurring-deposit (bank or India Post) premature closure or discontinuation rates; only the rules: India Post RD is discontinued after four missed monthly instalments (revivable within two months), with a Rs 1 per Rs 100 default fine per month
value: not published
unit: n/a
population: Indian bank and India Post recurring deposits
source_title: indiapost.org (unofficial explainer): Post Office RD Default and Revival 2026; Paisabazaar / BankBazaar RD guides
notes: Absence after two targeted searches (incl. CAG audit), not proof none exists. The 4-missed-instalments rule is a useful PRODUCT design reference: a daily product with 20/30 success means 10 misses a month, so 'still saving' must be defined (we define it as any successful debit in the month). Pigmy/daily-deposit retention: none found either.

claim: About 15 crore (26%) of 57.07 crore PM Jan Dhan accounts are inoperative (no customer-initiated transaction for over two years); 13.04 crore of 56.03 crore (23%) at 31 Jul 2025
unit: % of PMJDY accounts (count) with no customer-initiated transaction in 2+ years
population: All PM Jan Dhan Yojana accounts, India
source_title: Moneylife: Over 23% or 13 crore Jan Dhan accounts out of 56 crore are inactive (Govt, Lok Sabha reply); Daily Pioneer: 15 crore PM Jan Dhan accounts are inoperative
notes: WEAK analogue, recorded so nobody over-reads it: 'operative' only needs ONE customer transaction in two years, and DBT credits and RuPay use keep accounts alive. 74-77% 'operative' says nothing about regular saving. Shows the low bar official 'active' definitions use.

claim: Acorns (US micro-investing subscription): retains 99% of subscribers each month; 12-month retention 75% for the 2020 cohort vs 55% for the 2015 cohort; after the first 12 months retains nearly 80% for the next 5 years; 30% of leavers boomerang back within 12 months; biggest churn driver is subscribers not having enough money to save at a point in time
value: 55-75% at 12 months; ~1-1.3% monthly churn; 80% of 12-month survivors kept 5 years; 30% boomerang
unit: % of paying subscribers (count)
population: Acorns Grow Inc. subscribers, US, cohorts 2014-2020 (company claim in SPAC materials)
source_title: Pioneer Merger Corp / Acorns Form 425 investor materials (SEC EDGAR), 15 Sep 2021; S-4/A 2021 (via search summary)
notes: COMPANY CLAIM, US, much richer users, and a 'subscriber' pays a $1-5 monthly fee whether or not money is invested, so it OVERSTATES active saving. 12-month figures and the churn-driver line are from a search summary of the S-4; 99%/80%/30% confirmed on the EDGAR 425 page. Two lessons for us: (1) churn concentrates in year 1, then flattens (our churn_late 2%/month base is consistent with Acorns' ~1%); (2) about 30% of early leavers come BACK - our curve has no reactivation, which understates savers (and balances) in years 2-3. Treat as the bull ceiling; SPAC deal was terminated Jan 2022.

claim: Zomato CEO: 1.5 lakh to 2 lakh delivery workers leave the platform voluntarily every month and about 5,000 a month are terminated for fraud; Zomato onboards an equivalent number each month; many join to meet an immediate financial need and exit once it is met
value: 1.5-2 lakh voluntary exits per month on ~4.8 lakh monthly active partners (~31-42% a month, derived)
unit: delivery partners leaving per month (count); derived share of monthly active fleet
population: Zomato food-delivery partners, India (CEO statement on a podcast)
source_title: Storyboard18: Deepinder Goyal - Zomato terminates 5,000 delivery workers every month (also NewsBytes, NewsX)
notes: COMPANY CLAIM (spoken, not filed). The 4.8 lakh denominator is the search-summary figure (Eternal FY25 avg monthly active 4.73 lakh, SEG-06). 'Leave' may include riders who pause and return or move to another app, so platform exit != stopping saving. But it exposes a bias in INC-01: IDinsight's ~13-month average tenure is measured on CURRENTLY ACTIVE riders, which over-samples long stayers (length bias). The typical NEW rider - the one we acquire at a hub - stays far less. Gig base m3 48% / m6 33% may be optimistic if saving is tied to platform payouts (save_at_source channel).

claim: NPCI data for August 2025: 55-90% of automated payments on UPI AutoPay across public and private banks did not go through in the month, largely because of insufficient balances and incorrect beneficiary details
value: 55-90% failed (10-45% succeeded)
unit: % of UPI AutoPay execution attempts (count) failing, by remitter bank, one month
population: All UPI AutoPay mandate executions at major Indian remitter banks (all merchant categories), Aug 2025
source_title: Mint (via HT Syndication): UPI AutoPay's recurring woes are forcing an industry rethink
notes: ATTEMPT-level, not saver-level: merchants retry, so one successful debit can sit behind several failed attempts, and the mix is dominated by subscriptions/loan EMIs of Rs 100-1,000+, not Rs 40. Still the strongest warning found: our base assumes 20 of 30 daily debits succeed (67%) with one attempt + three retries. A search summary of other coverage says business declines averaged ~74% across the top 50 banks mid-2025 (unverified). If our attempt success is 30% and retries are correlated (same empty account), 20/30 is optimistic for riders paid weekly. Pilot must measure.

claim: More than 20 million UPI AutoPay mandates are revoked each month as users' accounts fall short of required balances; remitter banks recorded over 50 million new AutoPay mandate registrations in July 2025 (26 million in July 2024) and 808 million executions (392 million)
value: 20M+ revocations/month vs 50M+ new mandates/month
unit: mandates per month (count)
population: All UPI AutoPay mandates, India (NPCI data)
source_title: Business Standard: UPI autopay revocations hit 20 mn per month on low customer balance (via search summary; page 403)
notes: Search-summary figures; article body not readable. Roughly 2 revoked for every 5 created each month - mandate churn tied to LOW BALANCES is common at scale. For us a revoked mandate = a lost saver (re-mandating costs a new Rs 5-7.5 mandate and a re-activation effort). Supports a bear-ish debits_success and an early-month retention cliff.

claim: Gig-worker savings capacity: a LEAD at Krea University study found 62% of gig workers lacked an emergency fund and close to half had no insurance; coverage attributes to a 2024 NITI Aayog report the claim that 90% of gig workers lack savings
value: 62% no emergency fund; '90% lack savings' (attribution unverified)
unit: % of gig workers surveyed
population: Indian gig/platform workers (LEAD Krea sample; NITI attribution unclear)
source_title: Sahi blog / Drishti IAS editorial summarising LEAD (Krea) and NITI Aayog (via search summary)
notes: LOW QUALITY: secondary blogs; the '90% lack savings' line could not be traced to a NITI page and NITI's 2022 gig report is not known for it. Neither gives a rupee savings capacity. Confirms the starting point is near-zero liquid savings, which explains why debits bounce, but says nothing direct about Rs 25/40/60. Pigmy daily-deposit average tickets: not published (schemes advertise Rs 5-100 minimums only).

claim: Jar at an earlier stage: 'nearly 300,000 daily transactions' across 11 million users
value: ~300,000 transactions/day on 11M users; implies ~0.4M active savers = ~4% of registered (derived, using Jar's 22 saves/month claim)
unit: transactions per day (count); derived active-saver share of cumulative registered users
population: Jar app users, India (company-sourced figures, c. 2023)
source_title: Soul Startup (Substack): How Jar became India's go-to savings app
notes: DERIVED: 300k x 30 / 22 = ~409k savers; / 11M = 3.7%. With LEV-040 (1M txns/day on 20M+ users -> ~7%). The denominator is REGISTERED (installs that signed up), not activated savers, so it is not our ret_m24 - but the active share of everyone ever acquired sits at 4-7% across two points in time, which is what our CAC funnel x retention curve must reproduce. Our base: activation ~30-45% of installs x ~10-20% still saving after 1-2 years = ~4-8% of installs. Consistent, not generous. Undated blog; figures not attributed.

claim: Jar FY25 gold sales Rs 2,447.8 crore (statutory revenue incl. ~Rs 100 cr Nek jewellery) against 'over 1 million transactions every day' (claimed by Sep 2025) implies an average purchase of roughly Rs 64 or more per transaction
value: >= ~Rs 64 (derived)
unit: INR per gold purchase transaction (derived average, all frequencies incl. lump sums)
population: Jar users, FY25
source_title: Derived from Inc42 (Jar FY25 RoC filing) and TechCrunch/Deccan Chronicle transaction claim (market_benchmarks JAR-01, LEV-040)
notes: DERIVED: (2,447.8 - ~100 Nek) cr / (1M x 365) = ~Rs 64. A LOWER bound on the FY25 average because transactions were below 1M/day for most of FY25. Includes lump-sum and weekly/monthly buys, so the DAILY-save ticket is lower than the average. Our gig base Rs 40/debit is plausible for a daily auto-save; bull Rs 60 equals Jar's all-in average, i.e. high for a pure daily product.

claim: Groww customer acquisition cost: Rs 796 in H1 FY25, Rs 1,374 in H1 FY26 (+73%, driven by a 48% jump in performance marketing), Rs 900 in Q3 FY26; 81-84% of Groww customers were acquired organically (FY23-Q1 FY26, per RHP)
value: Rs 796 / Rs 1,374 / Rs 900 per new customer; 81-84% organic
unit: INR per newly acquired customer (company-reported CAC, definition not stated in coverage; blended incl. organic)
population: Groww (Billionbrains Garage Ventures) new customers, India, H1 FY25-Q3 FY26
source_title: Entrackr: Groww's customer acquisition cost spikes 73% in H1 FY26 (21 Nov 2025); Storyboard18: Groww cuts branding spend in Q3 FY26 as CAC falls 33%; Groww RHP organic share (via search summary)
notes: COMPANY-REPORTED, listed firm. India's largest investing app, with ~83% organic acquisition and a strong brand, still pays Rs 800-1,400 per new customer BLENDED. Paid-only CAC would be ~5-6x that if organic is free. Groww's customer is richer and wealth-seeking, and its 'customer' is likely a new TRANSACTING user (comparable to our 'activated'). Our base Rs 249 per activated saver is 3-5x below Groww's blended number. Our field channels can be cheaper than paid digital, but the gap needs a pilot, not an assumption.

claim: Vendor benchmarks for Android cost per install in India: fintech/finance median about Rs 75 ($0.80); UPI/payments Rs 30-80, lending Rs 80-200, wealth/broking Rs 100-300 per install
value: Rs 75 median; Rs 30-300 by sub-vertical
unit: INR per app install (paid UA, Android, India)
population: Indian fintech app paid user acquisition, 2025-2026 (vendor-compiled)
source_title: Linkrunner CPI benchmark tool; vmobify: App Install Cost India 2026 (via search summary)
notes: LOW QUALITY: ad-tech vendor blogs, methods unpublished; AppsFlyer's own India finance CPI not accessed. A savings/wealth app sits in the Rs 100-300 band, above our paid-digital channel's Rs 80 and well above our Rs 40-60 field 'cost per install'. Chained through our paid funnel (30% x 55% x 75% = 12% install-to-activation) a Rs 150 CPI gives ~Rs 1,200 + KYC per activated saver - consistent with our 'paid ads benchmark Rs 750' being optimistic.

claim: Jar marketing spend Rs 29.27 crore in FY24 (down 57% from FY23) and Rs 48.5 crore in FY25, against registered users growing from ~11M (2023) to 20M (Mar 2024) to 35M (Sep 2025) - roughly Rs 30-50 of marketing per NEW REGISTERED user
value: ~Rs 30-50 per new registered user (derived); Rs 29.27 cr FY24, Rs 48.5 cr FY25 marketing
unit: INR of marketing spend per net new registered user (derived; not per activated saver)
population: Jar (Central Square Fintech), FY24-FY25
source_title: Entrackr: Jar's revenue soars by 5.6X in FY24, marketing cost dips 57%; Inc42 FY25 (JAR-05); user counts JAR-07/LEV-040
notes: FY24 marketing figure is new; user counts repeat JAR-07/LEV-040. DERIVED: FY24 ~9M added / 29.27 cr = ~Rs 33; FY25 ~10M (interpolated 20M->35M over 18 months) / 48.5 cr = ~Rs 48. Per REGISTERED user, heavily organic (referrals, PhonePe distribution). If only 25-40% of registrants ever make a first save (unknown), marketing per ACTIVATED saver = Rs 80-200 - the closest real-world support for our Rs 249 base, and the best case: Jar is the category leader with brand pull and still excludes staff, KYC (gold needs none) and mandate costs. Note: gold needs no KYC, so Jar's funnel skips our biggest drop-off (install->KYC).

claim: Signicat 'Battle to Onboard': 68% of consumers abandoned a financial-services application (up from 63% in the prior edition); vendor UX blogs cite 40-60% abandonment during identity verification. No India-specific install->KYC or KYC->mandate funnel was found; one Indian product blog asserts '95% conversion success on mandate setup runs' with no source
value: 68% abandon (32% complete); India: not published
unit: % of consumers starting a financial-product application who abandon it
population: Consumers in Europe (Signicat survey); India not covered
source_title: Signicat Battle to Onboard (via vendor-blog search summary); productgrowth.in: UPI AutoPay - Designing Micro-Savings
notes: WEAK and non-Indian. 32% completion of a full application is in line with our install->KYC (40-70%) x KYC->mandate (55-85%) chain = 22-60% install->mandate; our BASE gig field channels sit at ~42-60%, the upper half. The 95% mandate figure is unsourced and refers to technical setup runs, not people. No Indian fintech publishes this funnel; it is the first thing a pilot must measure.

claim: Business correspondent (bank agent) payouts: savings-account opening commission typically Rs 10-100 per account (no national schedule; set by banks / corporate BCs); PMJJBY enrolment up to Rs 30; an older official estimate put account-opening cost at Rs 140 per account
value: Rs 10-100 per account opened; Rs 140 per account (older estimate); Rs 30 per PMJJBY enrolment
unit: INR paid per account opened / per insurance enrolment
population: Indian bank business correspondents (BC agents), PMJDY-era
source_title: HNR: BC Agent Commission Chart 2026 (blog); The Week (PTI): Business correspondents seek 30 bps hike in commission (28 Oct 2024); Business Standard 2015 (via search summary)
notes: LOW-MEDIUM quality (blog chart + search summary). The marginal field cost to SIGN SOMEONE UP in rural/low-income India is tens of rupees, consistent with our field 'cost per install' of Rs 50-60. But a BC-opened account is not a saver: a quarter of PMJDY accounts are inoperative (TB-10). The cost that matters is per ACTIVATED saver, which the BC system does not publish. Supports the INPUT costs, not the funnel.

claim: Government micro-insurance renewed by annual bank auto-debit: active enrolments about 8.3 crore (PMJJBY, Rs 436/yr life) and 23.9 crore (PMSBY, Rs 20/yr accident) around April 2023, against cumulative enrolments of 16.2 crore and 34.2 crore at the 8-year mark (May 2023)
value: ~51% (PMJJBY) and ~70% (PMSBY) of all-time enrolments still active after 8 years (derived)
unit: active policies / cumulative enrolments since 2015 (count, derived)
population: PMJJBY and PMSBY enrolees, India, via bank accounts
source_title: Business Standard (Apr 2023, via search summary: active 83M / 239M); PIB / AffairsCloud: PMJJBY, PMSBY & APY complete 8 years - 16.2 crore, 34.2 crore enrolments
notes: DERIVED ratio from two sources a month apart; the 'active' figure is a search summary. Not an annual renewal rate: a stock of 8 years of enrolments, many recent. Annual persistency behind a 51% stock ratio with growing enrolment is plausibly 70-85% - above our 55% base. BUT: premiums are tiny (Rs 20-436), renewal is a default auto-debit from a bank account, and banks are pushed by government to keep cover; non-renewal mostly comes from insufficient balance on the debit date. Our Rs 1,500-5,000 premium is 3-10x PMJJBY. Supports keeping ins_persist at 55% only if renewal is an auto-debit default; if renewal needs a fresh decision, use bear.

claim: Life-insurance 13th-month persistency FY25 (individual regular-premium policies): by NUMBER of policies, top-5 private insurers average 81% (best 83%) vs 64% for the comparison insurer shown (most likely LIC; logo not machine-readable), down 287 bps; by PREMIUM, 86% vs 75%
value: 64-83% by count; 75-88% by premium
unit: % of policies (count) paying the second-year premium, 13th month, 12 months to 31 Mar 2025
population: Individual life policies of Indian life insurers (excl. single premium), FY25, from insurers' public disclosures
source_title: Life Insurance Persistency Performance 31st Mar 2025 (industry compilation of public disclosures)
notes: Publisher not named in the extracted text (author metadata only). Agent-sold, long-term contracts where lapsing loses money - strong renewal incentives our 1-year health/accident/term covers lack. Count-based 64% for the mass-market insurer is the closest anchor; micro/group 1-year covers sold digitally renew worse. Our base 55% sits below every figure here, which is right for an embedded 1-year product to people whose saving itself stops (our renewal also requires the saver to still be active).

claim: PhonePe (insurance since Sep 2021) had sold over 9 million insurance policies in total, over 4 million in the last year (to Jan 2024); insurance + lending revenue Rs 557.6 crore in FY25
value: ~4M policies/year on a base of several hundred million users (~1-2% a year of users, derived and approximate)
unit: policies sold per year (count, all lines incl. motor, travel, health, life)
population: PhonePe users, India, 2023
source_title: Business Standard: PhonePe sells over 9 mn digital insurance policies, 4 mn in one year (18 Jan 2024); DRHP coverage (Statesman/Indian Startup News) for FY25 revenue
notes: COMPANY CLAIM. Denominator approximate (PhonePe claimed 500M+ registered users around then; monthly actives fewer) - so the annual purchase rate is very roughly 1-2% of users and lower still per unique buyer (policies != people). Our base ins_uptake 2% PER MONTH of eligible savers (~16% of active savers insured by month 12) is ~10x what India's largest payments app achieves per year. Our savers are a warmer, smaller audience with a trust relationship, but the burden of proof is on 16%.

claim: Embedded-insurance attach rates in India (vendor estimate): 3-6% at checkout for optional add-ons; 18-30% in lending journeys with inline consent, with personal-loan credit life often around 28%
value: 3-6% (optional add-on); 18-30% (bundled with a loan)
unit: % of transactions/loans with an insurance policy attached
population: Indian banks/NBFCs/e-commerce embedded insurance (vendor blog, unsourced)
source_title: Deployit: Embedded Insurance ROI for Banks and NBFCs - attach rate and persistency (via search summary)
notes: LOW QUALITY vendor blog, figures unsourced. Loan-bundled attach (18-30%) is inflated by lenders' pressure and is the practice IRDAI's 2026 draft targets with a 5% cap on loan-packaged commission (BM-10). A standalone, optional cover to savers sits nearer the 3-6% checkout band per offer. Our ~16% insured by m12 is achievable only if insurance is defaulted into the savings plan or tied to the loan.

claim: Swiggy, Zomato and Zepto already pay annual insurance premiums for their delivery partners at no deduction: Zomato medical cover of Rs 1 lakh for all delivery partners; Swiggy Rs 2 lakh accidental medical cover plus OPD; platforms collectively spent about Rs 100 crore on gig-worker insurance premiums in a year; workers report gaps between promised and usable cover
value: Rs 1-2 lakh platform-paid cover; ~Rs 100 crore/year premiums
unit: INR sum insured per partner; INR crore of premiums per year (all platforms)
population: Delivery partners of Swiggy, Zomato, Zepto, India
source_title: Inc42: Insurance Promises Vs Ground Reality - Gig Workers Push Back on Zomato, Swiggy Claims; Business Standard: Swiggy disbursed over Rs 31 cr in claims to delivery partners in FY22-23 (via search summary)
notes: Search-summary figures. The gig half's most obvious need (accident + hospital cover) is already given FREE by the platform, and the Social Security Code makes platform contributions mandatory. That SUBSTITUTES for our accident/health sale to riders; our pitch would be top-ups, family cover or term life, which convert worse. Suggests gig ins_uptake nearer bear (1%/month) than base; self-employed have no such cover, so their uptake could be higher.

claim: Co-holding: about 30% of US households co-hold high-cost debt and low-yield liquid assets (survey data); in UK transaction data co-holding occurs on ~15% of individual-days, and ~12% of UK households in another sample co-hold revolving credit and liquid assets
value: 12-30% of households
unit: % of households (or person-days) holding high-cost debt and liquid savings at the same time
population: US (Survey of Consumer Finances) and UK (bank transaction data) households
source_title: Gathergood & Olafsson, 'The Co-holding Puzzle: New Evidence from Transaction-Level Data', CEPR DP14799 (2020); Gathergood & Weber, JEBO 2014
notes: The best global evidence that SOME people borrow while holding savings they could use (mental accounting: 'that money is for X'). It is a MINORITY behaviour (12-30%), in rich countries, and about revolving cards, not a loan secured on the same savings. Supports that a secured-on-savings loan can find takers, framed as 'keep your savings growing / keep your streak', but does not support a high monthly application rate. No India data on borrowing against small liquid-fund balances was found.

claim: Indians increasingly borrow against their own gold rather than sell it: bank loans against gold jewellery rose 4.4x to Rs 5.52 lakh crore in July 2026 from Rs 1.24 lakh crore in July 2024 (+88.1% y/y); NBFC gold-backed lending ~Rs 3.54 lakh crore (+68.5% y/y); gold loans 7.7% of personal lending (RBI data)
value: Rs 5.52 lakh crore (banks) + Rs 3.54 lakh crore (NBFCs)
unit: INR outstanding (value)
population: Indian bank and NBFC gold-backed loans, July 2026 (RBI sectoral data)
source_title: ANI / Business Standard press release: Gold loans on the rise as Indians increasingly borrow against gold (22 Sep 2026)
notes: Press release (ANI) carrying RBI numbers. Strong evidence that low-income Indians prefer PLEDGING an asset to SELLING it - but jewellery has emotional value and is illiquid to sell; a liquid fund is not. The gold boom is also driven by price rise and by RBI tightening on unsecured credit. Our digital gold CANNOT back a loan [REG-023], so this behaviour helps us only if savers treat fund/FD money as 'not to be touched'. Plausible, unproven.

claim: Behaviour revealed in mobile-phone usage predicts loan repayment for unbanked borrowers: borrowers in the highest-risk quintile were 2.8 times more likely to default than those in the lowest; separately CGAP reports transaction-data-only models predict about as well as credit-history models, and better combined
value: 2.8x default, top vs bottom risk quintile
unit: ratio of default rates between risk quintiles (count)
population: Borrowers of a digital lender in a developing country (Björkegren & Grissen, World Bank Economic Review 2020); CGAP MSE transactional-data lending review
source_title: Björkegren & Grissen, 'Behavior Revealed in Mobile Phone Usage Predicts Credit Repayment' (SSRN/arXiv 1712.05840); CGAP: Leveraging Transactional Data for Micro and Small Enterprise Lending
notes: Supports the MECHANISM (regular behaviour data separates good from bad payers, like EVD-02 RappiCard) but is about phone usage, not saving. Still no study found that shows a SAVINGS streak lowers default for low-income borrowers in India; EVD-01 (US credit-builder RCT: ~40% of CBL users paid 30+ days late at least once) and EVD-03 (SHG NPA ~2% vs MFI, correlational) remain the only savings-specific evidence. Our ladder's 1.5% 90+ on unsecured money is founder data, not external.

Our base: loan_apply 4%/month x 50% eligible = ~2% of active savers applying each month, plus 2%/month insurance - roughly 10x Paytm's combined rate. Our savers are pre-qualified by a saving streak and the loan is secured, which should lift conversion, but the gap is large. The >50% repeat share of merchant-loan disbursal supports loan_repeat 45% (share of disbursal, not of repayers - not the same measure).

DEFINITION TRAP: Bajaj's 'cross-sell franchise' is the pool of customers it can cross-sell to (offer-eligible), not customers who bought a second product - so 63% is an ELIGIBILITY share, comparable at most to our loan_eligible (30/50/65%), not to loan_apply. Do not cite it as a conversion rate. Bajaj is a lender whose customers came for credit; ours came to save.

claim: When M-Shwari launched, a borrower's savings equal to the loan were 'frozen' to protect against default; 'this early policy was quickly changed and now savings are frozen only if the loan is in arrears for more than a day'. Customers said the main appeal of saving in M-Shwari was 'increasing access to credit in the future', not the interest rate
value: qualitative (design abandoned)
unit: n/a
population: M-Shwari (CBA + Safaricom), Kenya, 2012-2014
source_title: CGAP Forum: How M-Shwari Works - The Story So Far (Cook & McKay, Apr 2015), pp. 5-8
notes: Same CGAP family as CMP-04 but this detail is new to our files. The largest savings-linked digital lender in Africa STARTED with loans secured on the borrower's own savings - our loans 1-2 - and dropped it quickly (paper does not say why; plausibly low demand: why borrow your own money at 7.5%/month?). It then lent unsecured on a score. Direct warning on our ladder's first rungs. The upside: 'saving to become eligible for credit' was the main reason people saved - so the loan PROMISE may help retention even if the secured loan itself sells poorly.

claim: M-Shwari at Dec 2014: 9.2 million savings accounts opened, 4.7 million active in the last 90 days; 2.8 million unique borrowers since launch, 1.8 million active; average savings balance KES 504 (all accounts), KES 911 (active 90 days), KES 1,971 (active 30 days); NPL 2.2% over 90 days

unit: accounts (count); KES balance

source_title: CGAP Forum: How M-Shwari Works - The Story So Far (Apr 2015), p. 2 box
notes: Repeats CMP-04 with exact figures. 30% of all account openers borrowed at least once in ~2 years - but most opened the account TO borrow, and the loans were unsecured. Our base path (50% eligible x 4%/month among eligible never-borrowed) gives a cumulative share ever borrowing of the same order over 2 years - plausible only because M-Shwari's loan was the hook; ours is secured on savings, which M-Shwari abandoned. Active-30-day savers hold 4x the average balance: balances concentrate in a minority.

claim: NPCI NACH auto-debit bounce rates: in October 2021, 27 million of 86.6 million debit transactions initiated (31.24%) failed, described as back to pre-Covid levels; by value 24.83%; by May 2022 the value bounce rate eased to 22%

unit: % of NACH debit transactions (count / value) failing in a month
population: All NACH auto-debits in India (loan EMIs, SIPs, insurance premiums), NPCI data
source_title: Business Standard: Auto-debit bounce rates drop further in October to touch pre-Covid levels (Nov 2021); Unsuccessful auto-debit requests ease to a 38-month low in May (Jun 2022)
notes: Search-summary figures from two BS articles. A NORMAL-times national anchor: ~70% of monthly scheduled debits succeed across a mostly salaried, EMI-paying population. Our base 20/30 = 67% for DAILY debits from people paid daily/weekly sits right at this all-India average, i.e. it assumes our users are no worse than the average EMI payer - optimistic for riders, fair for shopkeepers with daily cash. Bull 24/30 = 80% beats the national NACH average: needs evidence. Retry policy changes the picture (a retry that succeeds later the same day helps), but attempts on an empty account fail together.

claim: Indian microfinance field economics: cost per borrower Rs 2,176-2,652 a year by MFI category (FY22, MFIN); pre-Covid a loan officer handled on average 556 borrowers; field-officer attrition reported at about 40%
value: Rs 2,176-2,652 per borrower per year; 556 borrowers per officer; ~40% officer attrition
unit: INR operating expense per active borrower per year; borrowers per loan officer; % annual staff attrition
population: Indian microfinance institutions (MFIN members), FY2021-22; loan-officer panel study (PMC)
source_title: MFIN India Microfinance Review FY 2021-22 (via search summary); 'Microfinance loan officers before and during Covid-19: Evidence from India' (PMC8743426)
notes: Not an acquisition cost - a SERVICING cost for a field-relationship model (Rs 180-220 per borrower per month). Two lessons for our field channels: (1) low-income customers who stay engaged usually do so through repeated human contact, which costs far more than our Rs 5 support + Rs 4 tech per month; if our retention depends on agents, cost to serve rises; (2) 40% field-staff attrition means our Rs 25k/month agents doing 20 installs/day is a steady-state productivity number that ignores hiring and ramp-up.

claim: Stable Money (FD/bond marketplace): over 20 lakh users at its Series B, over 40 lakh users (Rs 5,000+ crore invested) by early 2026, 'over 50 lakh' in latest claims; FY25 advertising Rs 25.33 crore; target of 1,00,000+ new users a month by end-2026

notes: DERIVED and fragile: assumes ~13-20 lakh users added in the FY25 window (Series B date not confirmed). 'Users' may include sign-ups who never invested; per INVESTING user the cost is higher (Altcase said Rs 5,000 per transacting FD user, BM-04). Two real savings apps (Jar ~Rs 30-50, Stable Money ~Rs 125-200 per new user, both MARKETING ONLY, excl. staff/KYC) bracket our base Rs 249 per ACTIVATED saver only if 50%+ of their 'users' activate. That is unlikely, so our base sits at the optimistic edge.

claim: Self Financial (US credit-builder: a secured instalment loan whose proceeds sit in a locked savings account until repaid) claims more than 1 million customers and a 47-point average credit-score lift with its Credit Builder Account
value: 1M+ customers; +47 points (company claims)
unit: customers (count, cumulative); FICO points (average, method undisclosed)
population: Self Financial customers, United States
source_title: Sunrise Banks: How Self Financial is leading the way; MT Newswires interview with Self Financial (via search summary)
notes: COMPANY CLAIMS; the 47-point lift is likely among customers who stayed current (survivor bias) - contrast EVD-01's RCT: no average score effect and ~40% of CBL users paid 30+ days late at least once. Shows a 'borrow your own savings to build credit' product CAN reach a million users - but only where a credit score gates rent, jobs and cards (US). In India a score matters to gig workers mainly for the next loan, so the pitch must be 'this unlocks a bigger loan', i.e. the ladder itself. No Indian credit-builder product with published take-up was found.

claim: Gullak (UPI-autopay gold savings app) in its YC launch: grew from 0 to 40k transacting users in 60 days with a monthly GTV of $280K, growing 25% week on week; founders' thesis was '50 Mn Indians saving $2/day'
value: ~$7 per transacting user per month (~Rs 580 at ~Rs 83/$, derived) vs a $2/day thesis
unit: gross transaction value per transacting user per month (derived, USD/INR)
population: Gullak transacting users, India, first 60 days (company claim, c. 2022)
source_title: Y Combinator company page: Gullak Money (launch post)
notes: COMPANY CLAIM, early adopters, derived ratio (GTV/transacting users; exchange rate approximate). Actual saving of ~Rs 580 a month per transacting user was about 1/9 of the founders' own $2/day thesis (~Rs 5,000/month). Our base gig Rs 40 x 20 = Rs 800/month and self-employed Rs 50 x 22 = Rs 1,100/month are above this early-stage real figure. Lesson: users choose lower amounts than founders expect; our bear (Rs 25 x 15 = Rs 375/month) is not pessimistic.

claim: Pioneer Microinsurance (Philippines) with microfinance partner CARD: renewal rate of voluntary products doubled from 23% to 46% between 2015 and 2017 after a customer-centric redesign (reminders, early renewal, multi-term options); enrolments rose from 600,000 to 1.6 million, a penetration of close to 15% of CARD membership in Dec 2017, up from 7.6% in 2015
value: 23% -> 46% renewal; 7.6% -> ~15% penetration
unit: % of voluntary policies renewed (PMI's own retention formula); % of CARD microfinance members enrolled
population: Voluntary microinsurance (Sagip Plan, CARD Care) sold to CARD microfinance clients, Philippines, 2015-2017
source_title: CGAP Customer-Centric Guide case study: Pioneer Microinsurance - Building a Business around Customers
notes: The best low-income VOLUNTARY renewal anchor found: 23% before and 46% after a deliberate retention programme (PMI could not compute it exactly - no unique customer ID). Our ins_persist bear 40% / base 55% / bull 70%: base is ABOVE what a dedicated insurer reached after redesign; bear 40% is closer to 'good' practice. Penetration: ~15% of an established microfinance membership after years of agent selling - similar to our ~16% of active savers insured by month 12, which we reach in one year through an app. Our base is at the top of this evidence.

With Paytm's >50% repeat share of merchant-loan disbursal (TB-31), PM SVANidhi's 68% second-loan persistency (NG-014) and Bueno's 30-50% (founder), the weight of evidence says repaying borrowers come back; our 45% base looks reasonable, perhaps conservative.

claim: Borrowing against one's own mutual funds is rare in India: Volt Money (largest digital LAMF platform, acquired by DSP Finance 2026) onboarded more than 1.8 lakh retail customers with a book of about Rs 4,000 crore, against 5.34 crore unique MF investors (Mar 2025); the whole LAMF market is estimated at about USD 5.6 billion (2025) vs MF AUM of Rs 85.76 lakh crore (Jul 2026)
value: ~0.3% of unique MF investors ever borrowed via Volt; LAMF ~0.6% of MF AUM (derived, rough); avg Volt book per customer ~Rs 2.2 lakh
unit: customers / unique investors (count); loan book / AUM (value) - derived
population: Indian mutual-fund investors, 2025-2026
source_title: Indian Startup Times / NE India Broadcast: DSP Finance acquires Volt Money (Aug 2026); Spherical Insights LAMF market estimate (via search summary); AMFI unique investors
notes: Search-summary figures; market estimate from a market-research blog (low quality); Volt's count from acquisition coverage. Volt is one of several lenders (banks, Groww, Fibe also offer LAMF), so the true share is higher than 0.3% but almost surely low single digits. LAMF users are affluent (avg ~Rs 2 lakh). Direct evidence that even well-off investors rarely borrow against funds they can redeem. Our ladder's secured loans 1-2 against Rs 1,000-3,000 of liquid fund face the same logic in a sharper form (why borrow Rs 2,000 when you can withdraw it?). Supports bear loan_apply for loans 1-2.
